loText: Explain how risks can arise through outsourcing activities to third-party service providers and describe elements of an effective program to manage outsourcing risk.
question:
A CRO at a U.S. bank is reviewing a proposal to outsource specialised trade-finance document processing to a provider in Brazil.

| Item | Detail |
|---|---|
| Eligible providers worldwide | Two, both located in São Paulo |
| Host country conditions | Recent political unrest and new currency controls |
| Proposed contract value | BRL 48 million over four years |
| Provider service level achieved last year | 99.2% |

A committee member argues that the fact that both eligible providers are located in São Paulo is an example of country risk. Which assessment is most accurate?

options.A: The committee member is right, because geographic clustering of providers within a single foreign city is the defining feature of country risk.
options.B: The clustering of a limited number of providers in one location is concentration risk, while the conditions in Brazil give rise to country risk.
options.C: Both facts are concentration risk, because country risk arises only when a foreign provider fails to comply with the laws of its own country.
options.D: Both facts are operational risk, because the guidance’s definition of operational risk covers losses from external events affecting a provider.

solution:
CRO assessing whether two providers clustered in São Paulo represent country risk.

**Concept and theory**

Concentration risk and country risk both involve geography, which is why they are confused. The guidance separates them by mechanism:

| Risk | Trigger in GARP 12.2 | Question to ask |
|---|---|---|
| Concentration | services provided by a limited number of providers or concentrated in limited geographic locations | How many alternatives do we have, and are they all in the same place? |
| Country | a foreign-based provider exposes the bank to economic, social and political conditions and events in its country | What could happen in that country that disrupts the provider? |
| Operational | inadequate or failed processes or systems, external events, human error at the provider | Did the provider’s processes, systems or people fail? |

Concentration is about the structure of supply (few providers, clustered locations), and it can arise entirely within one’s own country. Country risk is about the host-country environment and requires a foreign-based provider. Operational risk’s “external events” does not absorb either: the guidance names country and concentration as distinct risks precisely so that these channels are assessed separately.

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question:
The head of third-party risk at a Singapore bank is drafting an internal standard that sets how deep and how formal the due diligence on each prospective service provider must be. Her draft lists the following factors:

I. The scope, complexity and importance of the planned outsourcing arrangement.

II. The bank’s familiarity with the prospective service providers.

III. The reputation and industry standing of the service provider.

IV. The total number of material business activities the bank outsources across all of its service providers.

Which of the factors does the Federal Reserve guidance identify as determining the depth and formality of the due diligence performed on a prospective service provider?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: I and III only
options.C: I, II and III only
options.D: I, II, III and IV

solution:
Head of third-party risk at a Singapore bank listing the factors that set the depth and formality of due diligence.

**Concept and theory**

Due diligence is the second core element of a service provider risk management program. It is the evaluation an institution performs on a prospective provider before engaging it, to establish whether that provider can deliver the service safely, soundly and in compliance with the law. The guidance is deliberately proportional: it does not prescribe one fixed procedure for every provider. Instead it says the depth and formality of due diligence “will vary” with three named drivers.

| Driver named in GARP | Why it changes the effort required |
|---|---|
| Scope, complexity and importance of the planned arrangement | A critical, complex arrangement can hurt the institution more if the provider fails, so it warrants a deeper, more formal review. |
| Institution’s familiarity with prospective providers | Existing knowledge of a provider reduces the information gap that due diligence is meant to close. |
| Reputation and industry standing of the provider | A long-established, reputable provider carries less selection uncertainty than an unknown one. |

Be careful to keep this list separate from a similar list one level up. GARP also says that the depth and formality of the whole risk management program depends on the criticality, complexity and […]

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question:
An internal auditor at a German bank is reviewing the file for a recently outsourced loan servicing activity. The file records the following sequence of steps.

| Step | Date (2026) |
|---|---|
| Risk assessment approves outsourcing the activity | 3 February |
| Contract signed and provider engaged (annual fee EUR 4.5 million) | 10 March |
| References checked and financial statements reviewed, filed as “due diligence” | 2 to 20 May |
| Service Organization Control 2 report requested from the provider | 15 June |

Which of the following conclusions should the auditor reach?

options.A: The file is compliant, because due diligence and ongoing monitoring form a single element, so the order of the steps is immaterial.
options.B: The file is deficient, because due diligence should be performed before engaging the provider; reviews made after signing are monitoring.
options.C: The file is deficient, because due diligence on prospective providers should precede the risk assessment of whether to outsource at all.
options.D: The file is compliant, provided the Service Organization Control 2 report is received within the first year of the engagement.

solution:
Internal auditor at a German bank reviewing a file in which “due diligence” was done after the contract was signed.

**Concept and theory**

The guidance arranges the service provider risk management program as a logical sequence. First comes the risk assessment: is outsourcing the activity consistent with strategy, what are its benefits, risks and costs, are qualified providers available, and can the institution oversee the relationship? Only once outsourcing is judged appropriate does the institution select a provider, and selection is where due diligence sits. GARP is explicit on timing: the institution “should conduct an evaluation of and perform the necessary due diligence for a prospective service provider prior to engaging the service provider.” Contract negotiation, incentive compensation review, and ongoing oversight and monitoring follow.

| Element | Question it answers | When |
|---|---|---|
| Risk assessment | Should we outsource this activity at all? | Before any provider is chosen |
| Due diligence | Is this prospective provider fit to perform it? | Before engaging the provider |
| Oversight and monitoring | Is the engaged provider still performing? | Throughout the relationship |

Why does timing matter? The purpose of due diligence is to inform the selection decision. A review carried out after the contract is signed cannot affect which provider was selected; i […]

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question: A risk committee member at a Japanese regional bank asks the head of procurement who should take part in the due diligence on a prospective provider of core banking software, a JPY 900 million arrangement. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.A: Every department of the bank should sign off on each due diligence review, whatever the scope and importance of the planned arrangement.
options.B: The bank’s technical experts should contribute to the review but be kept out of approval, so that approval stays independent of the review.
options.C: Once due diligence confirms the provider’s legal compliance, responsibility for the compliance of the outsourced service passes to the provider.
options.D: The bank’s technical experts and key stakeholders should be engaged in the review and approval process, as needed, throughout due diligence.

solution:
Risk committee member at a Japanese regional bank asking who should take part in due diligence on a core banking software provider.

**Concept and theory**

Due diligence is the institution’s own evaluation, and GARP names who inside the institution should be involved: “Throughout the due diligence process, financial institution technical experts and key stakeholders should be engaged in the review and approval process as needed.” Three features of that sentence carry weight.

- Who: the institution’s own technical experts (for example IT, information security, legal) and key stakeholders (for example the business line that will depend on the service).
- Which stages: both the review and the approval; experts are not merely consulted and then excluded.
- How much: “as needed”, which is consistent with the proportional design of due diligence.

Separately, the guidance never transfers accountability. The use of service providers does not relieve the board and senior management of their responsibility to ensure outsourced activities are safe, sound and compliant, and under operations and internal controls GARP states that institutions are responsible for ensuring that services provided by service providers comply with applicable laws and regulations.

question:
A junior risk analyst at a US bank holding company has sorted items from a due diligence checklist into the three review areas set out in the Federal Reserve guidance. Her assignments are shown below.

| Checklist item | Review area assigned |
|---|---|
| Provider’s commitment of staff resources for the contract’s duration | Operations and internal controls |
| Verification of required licences and certifications | Business background, reputation and strategy |
| Maintenance and retention of records | Operations and internal controls |
| Adequacy of the provider’s insurance coverage | Financial performance and condition |

Which of the following assignments is NOT consistent with the guidance?

options.A: Commitment of staff resources for the contract’s duration, assigned to operations and internal controls.
options.B: Verification of required licences and certifications, assigned to business background, reputation and strategy.
options.C: Maintenance and retention of records, assigned to operations and internal controls.
options.D: Adequacy of the provider’s insurance coverage, assigned to financial performance and condition.

| Area | Question it answers | Representative items in GARP |

Business background, reputation and strategy | Who is this provider and is its model durable? | Industry status, corporate history, qualifications; principals; employee background check program; experience; business model; references; licences and certifications; pending legal or regulatory issues |

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question: A risk consultant is presenting the Federal Reserve due diligence guidance to newly hired analysts at a bank holding company. An analyst asks where checks on the provider’s personnel appear in the three review areas. Which of the following answers best describes the guidance?

options.A: Background checks sit only under financial performance and condition, as part of the provider’s commitment of staff resources to the contract.
options.B: Under business background, the bank ensures the provider has an appropriate employee background check program; the operations review may also cover employee background checks.
options.C: Under business background, the bank itself carries out background checks on every provider employee who will be assigned to its account.
options.D: Background checks sit only under operations and internal controls; the business background area reviews only the background of the provider’s principals.

solution:
Risk consultant explaining to new analysts where checks on the provider’s personnel appear in the three due diligence areas.

**Concept and theory**

Personnel risk at a provider is a real source of operational loss: an employee with a history of fraud who gains access to customer data or payment systems can cause damage no control framework fully offsets. The guidance therefore touches personnel checks twice, from two different angles.

| Area | GARP wording | Angle |
|---|---|---|
| Business background, reputation and strategy | “ensure that the service provider has an appropriate background check program for its employees”; also review “the background and reputation of the service provider and its principals” | Does the provider have a program? Who are its principals? |
| Operations and internal controls | “Employee background checks” among the items that may need review | Are checks actually being performed in operating the activity? |

The first is a check on the provider’s policies and its leadership; the second is a check on operating practice. Schweser expresses the same split: under business background the provider “should provide evidence of an adequate background check system for its new employees”, and under operations and internal controls the institution seeks “confirmation that employee background checks are being performed.”

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question: A treasurer at an Australian bank is preparing a report to the outsourcing committee on the business background, reputation and strategy of a prospective cash management provider. Which of the following statements should the treasurer include in the report?

options.A: Reference checks are used mainly to establish the provider’s capital strength and liquidity before the contract is signed.
options.B: The search for pending litigation, regulatory actions or complaints can be confined to the provider entity, leaving its principals aside.
options.C: The provider’s experience with the proposed service is evaluated mainly to benchmark the fee the bank will be charged for it.
options.D: The resiliency and adaptability of the provider’s business model are factors in assessing its future viability to perform the services.

solution:
Treasurer at an Australian bank preparing a report on the business background, reputation and strategy of a cash management provider.

**Concept and theory**

The business background, reputation and strategy review answers the question “who is this provider, and will its business still be able to serve us in the future?” GARP builds the review from the following components.

| Component | What is reviewed and why |
|---|---|
| Industry status and history | Status in the industry, corporate history and qualifications. |
| People | Background and reputation of the provider and its principals; an appropriate employee background check program. |
| Experience | Experience in providing the proposed service, “in order to assess its qualifications and competencies to perform the service”. |
| Business model | Business strategy and mission, service philosophy, quality initiatives and organisational policies. |
| Future viability | “The resiliency and adaptability of the service provider’s business model as factors in assessing the future viability of the provider to perform services.” |
| References | Checked “to ascertain its performance record”. |
| Licences | Verify any required licences and certifications. |
| Legal and compliance issues | Pending litigation, regulatory actions or complaints associated with the provider and its principals. |

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question:
A senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank is reviewing a colleague’s notes on the business background, reputation and strategy review of a prospective payroll provider. The notes contain these statements:

I. The review should cover the provider’s status in the industry, its corporate history and its qualifications.

II. The bank should verify whether there are pending legal or regulatory compliance issues associated with the provider and its principals.

III. Verification of required licences and certifications may be omitted where the provider’s references report a strong performance record.

IV. The provider’s service philosophy, quality initiatives and organisational policies are evaluated as part of its business model.

Which of the statements are consistent with the guidance?

options.A: I, II and IV only
options.B: I and II only
options.C: II, III and IV only
options.D: I, II, III and IV

solution:
Senior risk analyst at a Canadian bank auditing four statements about the business background review of a payroll provider.

**Concept and theory**

The business background, reputation and strategy review (see the component table in Solution

6) combines several independent checks. The important design feature is that the checks are cumulative: each addresses a different failure mode, so a strong result on one does not excuse another. References tell the institution how the provider has performed for others. Licence and certification verification tells it whether the provider is legally permitted and qualified to perform the service at all. A provider can have excellent references and still be unlicensed for the activity, or have a licence under threat because of a pending regulatory action. GARP therefore lists the checks side by side: “Financial institutions should check the service provider’s references to ascertain its performance record, and verify any required licenses and certifications.”

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question:
A risk analyst at a UK bank is reviewing the financial performance and condition of a prospective provider of mortgage document processing. She has gathered the following data.

| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Provider annual revenue (GBP million) | 48.0 |
| Proposed annual contract value (GBP million) | 9.6 |
| Provider years in business | 3.0 |
| Provider insurance cover (GBP million) | 5.0 |
| Bank total assets (GBP million) | 12 000.0 |

Which of the following conclusions is most consistent with the guidance on the financial review of a prospective service provider?

options.A: The bank’s total assets of GBP 12.0 billion are a key input, since the review assesses the impact of the provider on the bank’s own financial condition.
options.B: The three-year operating history can be set aside, since the provider’s sustainability is judged only by its growth of market share for the service.
options.C: The contract would be 20% of the provider’s revenue, which matters because the review considers the impact of the bank’s relationship on the provider’s finances.
options.D: The GBP 5.0 million insurance cover can be set aside at this stage, since insurance is addressed only through the insurance provision of the contract.

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question: A treasury analyst at a Chinese bank is planning the financial review of a prospective payments processor for a CNY 60 million arrangement. The processor is a subsidiary within a larger group and relies on two subcontractors for parts of the service. Which of the following approaches is most consistent with the guidance?

options.A: Review the contracting entity alone, since its affiliates and subcontractors are addressed only through the contract’s subcontracting provision.
options.B: Review the processor and its affiliates, and rely on the subcontractors’ own review of the processor’s financial condition.
options.C: Review the processor’s affiliates only if its insurance coverage proves inadequate, and its subcontractors only after the contract is signed.
options.D: Review the processor and its closely-related affiliates, and assess the adequacy of the processor’s review of its subcontractors’ financial condition.

solution:
Treasury analyst at a Chinese bank planning the financial review of a group-owned payments processor that uses subcontractors.

**Concept and theory**

A provider’s financial strength rarely stops at its own legal entity. Two extensions matter.

- Affiliates. A subsidiary may depend on its group for funding, shared services or guarantees, and group distress can pass down to it. GARP therefore opens the financial review with: “Financial institutions should review the financial condition of the service provider and its closely-related affiliates.”
- Subcontractors. If parts of the service are subcontracted, a subcontractor’s failure can interrupt the service just as surely as the provider’s own failure. GARP’s response is layered: the institution reviews “the adequacy of the service provider’s review of the financial condition of any subcontractors.” In other words, the provider is expected to vet its subcontractors, and the institution evaluates whether that vetting is adequate.

The layered design reflects the structure of accountability elsewhere in the guidance: in the contract, the primary provider has overall accountability for all services that it and its subcontractors provide, and agreements should include the provider’s process for assessing the subcontractor’s financial condition.

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question: An internal auditor at a Swiss bank is validating the due diligence policy for outsourcing. The policy states: “For every outsourced activity, each item in the operations and internal controls checklist must be reviewed in full, whatever the activity.” Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate?

options.A: Retain the policy as written, because the guidance requires every operations and internal controls item to be reviewed for every outsourced activity.
options.B: Revise the policy, because some or all items may need review depending on the activity, while the bank stays responsible for compliance and safe-and-sound practice.
options.C: Revise the policy, because the operations and internal controls review is needed only where the outsourced activity involves information technology services.
options.D: Revise the policy, because a provider’s written confirmation that it adheres to laws may replace the review, as compliance responsibility rests with the provider.

solution:
Internal auditor at a Swiss bank validating a policy that requires every operations and internal controls item for every activity.

**Concept and theory**

The operations and internal controls review answers: “will this provider run the activity safely and lawfully?” GARP frames it in three steps.

1. Responsibility. “Financial institutions are responsible for ensuring that services provided by service providers comply with applicable laws and regulations and are consistent with safe-and-sound banking practices.”
2. General test. “Financial institutions should evaluate the adequacy of standards, policies, and procedures.”
3. Tailored item list. “Depending on the characteristics of the outsourced activity, some or all of the following may need to be reviewed”: internal controls; facilities management (such as access requirements or sharing of facilities); training, including compliance training for staff; security of systems (for example, data and equipment); privacy protection of the institution’s confidential information; maintenance and retention of records; business resumption and contingency planning; systems development and maintenance; service support and delivery; employee background checks; and adherence to applicable laws, regulations and supervisory guidance.

question: A senior analyst at a Brazilian bank is drafting the operations and internal controls section of a due diligence report on a prospective provider that would run a customer call centre handling the bank’s confidential information. Which of the following statements is most accurate for inclusion in the report?

options.A: Business resumption and contingency planning lies outside due diligence and is reviewed only once the contract has been signed.
options.B: Service support and delivery is assessed under financial performance and condition, since it depends on the provider’s staff resources.
options.C: Privacy protection of the bank’s confidential information and the maintenance and retention of records are among the items to review.
options.D: Systems development and maintenance need not be reviewed, since the provider rather than the bank owns and runs the call centre systems.

See Solution 10 for the structure of the operations and internal controls review. The point here is content: which items belong to the operations list, and which belong elsewhere. The table sorts the operations items by the risk they address.

| Risk addressed | Operations and internal controls items in GARP |
|---|---|
| Control environment | Internal controls; adherence to applicable laws, regulations and supervisory guidance |
| Physical and people | Facilities management (access requirements, sharing of facilities); training, including compliance training; employee background checks |

loText: Explain how financial institutions should perform due diligence on third-party service providers.
question:
A board risk committee member at an Australian bank is reviewing a post-incident report on an outsourced mortgage document processing service.

- Before engagement, the bank reviewed the provider’s audited financial statements, confirmed its insurance cover, assessed its internal controls and IT security, and reviewed its tested business continuity plan.
- The bank did not verify the provider’s licence status and did not check for regulatory actions involving the provider’s two founding directors.
- Six months after go-live, the regulator suspended the provider’s licence following an enforcement action against the directors that had been pending at the time of selection. Services stopped and the bank incurred AUD 3.1 million of remediation costs.

Which of the following best describes the due diligence lesson from this case?

options.A: The business background review should have verified the required licences and checked for pending regulatory issues involving the provider and its principals.
options.B: The financial performance and condition review should have assessed the potential impact of the bank’s business relationship on the provider’s financial condition.
options.C: The operations and internal controls review should have covered business resumption and contingency planning, so that the stoppage could have been foreseen.
options.D: The gap lay in oversight and monitoring, because escalation triggers after go-live would have prevented the bank from selecting this provider.

solution:
Board risk committee member at an Australian bank reviewing a case where a provider’s licence was suspended after go-live.

**Concept and theory**

The three due diligence areas are designed so that each catches a different kind of provider failure. Diagnosing a case therefore means asking: which area, done properly, would have revealed the fact that later caused the loss?

| Area | Failure it is designed to catch |
|---|---|
| Business background, reputation and strategy | Provider not qualified or not permitted to act (licences, certifications); reputation or integrity problems with the provider or its principals; pending litigation, regulatory actions or complaints; a fragile business model |
| Financial performance and condition | Provider unable to fund delivery for the contract term; excessive dependence on the institution’s business; inadequate insurance; weak subcontractor vetting |
| Operations and internal controls | Weak controls, security, privacy, records, continuity or service delivery in running the activity |

Due diligence is pre-engagement. Oversight and monitoring (program element E), including escalation triggers, operates after engagement; it can detect deterioration but cannot change a selection decision already made on incomplete information.

loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
question:
The head of vendor management at a U.S. state member bank is presenting to newly hired analysts on the contracting stage of the bank’s service provider risk management programme. Her slides contain the following statements:

I. The terms of a service agreement should be set out in a written contract that the bank’s legal counsel has reviewed before the contract is executed.

II. The scope provision should define the rights and responsibilities of each party, including compliance with applicable laws, regulations and regulatory guidance.

III. For a routine activity, the contract terms should follow a standard template that does not depend on the characteristics of the activity or on the provider’s strategy for delivering it.

IV. The scope provision should address the distribution of any required statements or disclosures to the service provider’s own shareholders.

Which of the statements are correct?

options.A: I only
options.B: I and II only
options.C: I, II and IV only
options.D: II and III only

solution:
Head of vendor management presenting four statements on the contracting stage and the scope provision.

**Concept and theory**

An outsourcing contract is the instrument that turns the institution’s expectations of a service provider into enforceable obligations. The guidance (Federal Reserve SR 13-19) treats “contract provisions and considerations” as one of six core elements of a service provider risk management programme, sitting after risk assessment and due diligence. Its starting points are procedural. First, the institution should understand the service contract and the legal issues of the proposed arrangement, and the terms of service should be defined in written contracts that the institution’s legal counsel has reviewed before execution. Second, the contract is not generic: the characteristics of the business activity being outsourced and the provider’s strategy for providing those services determine the terms of the contract.

The first substantive provision is **scope**: contracts should clearly define the rights and responsibilities of each party. GARP lists the matters the scope provision includes:

| Scope items (GARP) | What they settle |
|---|---|
| Support, maintenance and customer service | What the provider must keep running |
| Contract timeframes | Duration of the obligations |
| Compliance with applicable laws, regulations and regulatory guidance | Legal  […]

question:
An internal auditor at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing the cost and compensation clause of a draft loan servicing agreement. The draft contains the following terms:

| Item | Draft treatment |
|---|---|
| Monthly base fee | USD 45,000, fixed |
| Per-loan boarding charge | USD 12 per loan boarded |
| Non-recurring items and special requests | “To be agreed informally when they arise” |
| Legal, audit and examination fees for the activity | Not addressed |
| Servicer’s long-term credit rating | BBB |

Which of the following recommendations is most appropriate?

options.A: Remove the per-loan boarding charge, since compensation for an outsourced activity should be limited to a fixed fee that does not vary with volume.
options.B: Leave the examination fees unaddressed, since fees relating to supervisory examinations fall outside the contract and are settled with the regulator.
options.C: Require the servicer to bear all equipment, hardware and software costs, since the guidance assigns these expenses to the service provider by default.
options.D: Describe the fees for non-recurring items and special requests, and state which party pays the legal, audit and examination fees related to the activity.

loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
question: A junior risk analyst at a savings and loan holding company is drafting a summary of the right to audit provision for a new payments processing agreement. Which of the following statements best describes the provision?

options.A: The agreement may give the institution or its representatives the right to audit the provider and/or to access its audit reports, and should define the types of reports and the frequency of the audits and reports.
options.B: The agreement must give the institution an on-site right to audit the provider, since access to the provider’s audit reports cannot substitute for an audit by the institution or its representatives.
options.C: The agreement should give the provider a reciprocal right to audit the institution’s processes connected with the service, so that oversight under the contract runs in both directions.
options.D: The agreement may give the institution a right to audit the provider, with the types of audit reports and their frequency to be settled after execution as issues come to light.

solution:
Junior risk analyst summarising the right to audit provision for a payments processing agreement.

**Concept and theory**

Outsourcing moves an activity out of the reach of the institution’s own internal audit. The **right to** **audit** provision restores visibility. GARP: agreements may provide for the right of the institution or its representatives to audit the service provider and/or to have access to audit reports; agreements should define the types of audit reports the institution will receive and the frequency of the audits and reports. Three features matter:

| Feature | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Strength | Permissive: “may provide”; this is the provision the guidance frames as optional |
| Who audits | The institution or its representatives (for example external auditors) |
| Form | An audit right, access to audit reports, or both (“and/or”) |
| What must be defined | Types of audit reports and frequency of audits and reports |

The right is one-directional: it protects the institution, which remains responsible for the outsourced activity. Later, under oversight (part E), the institution decides when to exercise the right as part of escalation, which is why the reports and frequency need to be fixed in the contract in advance.

options.C: Replace both items with measurable performance standards, for example a stated monthly availability percentage and a maximum time to respond to an incident.
options.D: Replace both items with standards that the provider may set and revise at its discretion, provided it informs the bank of each change in its annual report.

CRO reviewing vague availability and incident wording in an online banking service schedule.

A provider cannot be held to a promise that cannot be measured. The provision on **establishment** **and monitoring of performance standards** says agreements should define measurable performance standards for the services or products being provided. Measurable standards serve three later purposes: they let the institution monitor performance (part E says the institution should establish acceptable performance metrics that the business line or relationship management regards as indicative of acceptable performance); they define when the provider is failing; and they feed the default and termination provision, which lists “failure to meet performance standards” among termination rights. Without numbers, none of these mechanisms works.

“High availability” and “promptly” are qualitative. The deciding fact is the word measurable. The annual fee of USD 1.2 million is an irrelevant input: it belongs to cost and compensation and does not affect what the performance clause must contain. The fix is to replace the adjectives with quantities, such as an availability percentage per month and a maximum response time.

loText: Describe topics and provisions that should be addressed in a contract with a third-party service provider.
question: A senior risk analyst at a U.S. state member bank is preparing a report on an incident at the provider that processes the bank’s outgoing wire transfers. A provider employee negligently sent customer payments to the wrong beneficiaries, and several customers have now filed claims against the bank. Which of the following provisions, as described, should the bank’s contract have contained to address the bank’s position?

options.A: A customer complaints provision, making the provider liable for any customer claim relating to a complaint that the provider has handled.
options.B: An indemnification provision, requiring the bank to indemnify the provider against claims caused by the provider’s negligence.
options.C: An indemnification provision, requiring the provider to indemnify the bank against all claims connected with the activity, whatever their cause.
options.D: An indemnification provision, requiring the provider to indemnify the bank against claims against the bank resulting from the provider’s negligence.

solution:
Senior risk analyst reporting on negligent misrouting of wires at a provider and resulting customer claims.

**Concept and theory**

When a provider acts for an institution, the institution’s customers usually pursue the institution, not the provider, because the customer’s contract is with the bank. **Indemnification** reallocates that loss back to the party at fault. GARP: agreements should provide for service provider indemnification of financial institutions for any claims against financial institutions resulting from the service provider’s negligence. Four elements, each a possible trap:

| Element | Guidance |
|---|---|
| Who indemnifies | The service provider |
| Who is protected | The financial institution |
| What is covered | Claims against the institution |
| Trigger | Resulting from the service provider’s negligence |

Indemnification is distinct from limits on liability (which caps what the provider pays) and from insurance (which funds the provider’s ability to pay).

**Applying it to this question**

The facts supply every element: the provider’s employee acted negligently, customers filed claims against the bank, and the bank wants to recover. The correct option must name indemnification, run from provider to bank, and be triggered by the provider’s negligence.

options.B: The provider will maintain adequate insurance, provide the bank with proof of insurance, and notify the bank when there is a material change in its coverage.
options.C: The provider will maintain adequate insurance; since adequacy was verified during due diligence, the provider need not report later changes in its coverage.
options.D: The provider will maintain insurance equal to the full contract value, which makes a separate indemnification provision in the agreement unnecessary.

Treasurer reviewing the insurance clause of a cash logistics agreement.

**Concept and theory**

Insurance appears twice in the outsourcing guidance, at two different stages, and the distinction is a favourite trap. At due diligence (LO 53.b), the institution reviews “the adequacy of the service provider’s insurance coverage” as part of financial performance and condition: a one-off assessment before signing. In the contract, the **insurance** provision creates continuing obligations: service providers should have adequate insurance and provide financial institutions with proof of insurance, and should notify financial institutions when there is a material change in their insurance coverage. The notification duty exists precisely because coverage verified at selection can lapse or shrink during the term. Insurance also appears as a scope item (“insurance coverage requirements”).

**Applying it to this question**

A compliant clause needs three components, all on the provider: (1) adequate insurance, (2) proof of insurance, (3) notification of material changes. Check each option for all three and for any added claim.

**Fragile fact.** Adequacy of insurance is reviewed at due diligence; in the contract the provider must hold adequate cover, give proof, and notify the institution of any material change.

question: A portfolio manager at the asset management subsidiary of a U.S. bank holding company is negotiating an agreement with a provider of performance analytics. The provider will receive client holdings data, generate risk scores from it, and has asked to use the data to improve products it sells to other clients. Which of the following best describes how the agreement should deal with these matters?

options.A: The ownership and license provision should establish that information the provider generates from the institution’s data belongs to the provider.
options.B: The confidentiality and security provision should settle who owns the information the provider generates, as part of limiting the provider’s access to data.
options.C: The ownership and license provision should define when the provider may use institution property, including data, and address ownership and control of information it generates.
options.D: The ownership and license provision should prohibit the provider from using the institution’s data, hardware, software or intellectual property in any circumstances.

solution:
Portfolio manager negotiating use of holdings data and ownership of derived risk scores with an analytics provider.

**Concept and theory**

Two property questions arise in almost every outsourcing arrangement: may the provider use what the institution gives it, and who owns what the provider creates? The **ownership and license** provision answers both. GARP: agreements should define the ability and circumstances under which service providers may use financial institution property, inclusive of data, hardware, software and intellectual property; and agreements should address the ownership and control of any information generated by service providers. (The same provision also covers software escrow, tested in Q10.) The design is deliberately neither permissive nor prohibitive: the provider often needs to use institution data to perform the service, so the contract defines when and how, rather than banning use. Separately, ownership of derived output must be settled expressly, because by default a provider may claim it.

**Applying it to this question**

The stem raises both questions: use of client holdings data (including for the provider’s other clients) and ownership of generated risk scores. The correct option must name ownership and license and must cover both halves without a ban or a pre-emptive award of ownership.

A treasury analyst at the U.S. operations of a German bank is reviewing the purchase of proprietary treasury management software from a small vendor. The analyst has gathered the following information:

| Item | Detail |

| Annual support fee | EUR 120,000 |
| Vendor’s years in business | 4 |
| Source code | Proprietary, held only by the vendor |

question: A risk consultant is advising a community bank on the default clause of an agreement to outsource its loan review function. Which of the following draft clauses is most consistent with the guidance?

options.A: Any breach of any term is an immediate default, giving the bank the right to terminate at once without notice and without any opportunity for the provider to cure.
options.B: The agreement defines the events that constitute a contractual default, lists acceptable remedies, and provides opportunities for the provider to cure a default.
options.C: The provider defines the events that constitute a default and the related remedies, since it is best placed to judge what its own operations can deliver.
options.D: Events of default are not defined in the agreement but are determined case by case under the dispute resolution process when a disagreement arises.

solution:
Risk consultant advising on the default clause of a loan review outsourcing agreement.

**Concept and theory**

Termination is costly and disruptive for both sides, so the guidance asks for a graduated path. The first half of the **default and termination** provision deals with default. GARP: agreements should define events of a contractual default, provide a list of acceptable remedies, and provide opportunities for curing default. This creates a sequence:

defined default event ⇒ acceptable remedies and cure period ⇒ termination right if not cured

Defining events in advance avoids arguments over whether a default has occurred; listing remedies lets the institution respond proportionately; cure opportunities preserve a service the institution depends on. The second half of the provision (termination rights, transition and return of data) is tested in Q12.

**Applying it to this question**

The test is whether the clause has the three components (defined events, acceptable remedies, cure opportunities) and whether the institution’s agreement, rather than the provider or a later process, defines them.

**Fragile fact.** Default comes with remedies and an opportunity to cure before termination; the events are defined in the agreement, in advance.

| Group | Termination rights listed by GARP |
|---|---|
| Ownership changes | Change in control; merger or acquisition |
| Commercial terms | Increase in fees |
| Performance and obligations | Failure to meet performance standards; failure to fulfil contractual obligations; failure to provide required notices |
| Legal and viability | Failure to prevent violations of law; bankruptcy, closure or insolvency |

Contracts should also include termination and notification requirements that give the institution sufficient time to transfer services to another service provider, and should address the provider’s preservation and timely return of the institution’s data, records and other resources. The motivation is continuity: the institution must be able to exit without losing service or data.

Ownership events are included because a new owner may change strategy, staffing or financial strength, all of which were assessed at due diligence.

question: The chief compliance officer of a regional bank is dealing with a billing disagreement with its domestic mortgage subservicer. The subservicer has threatened to stop servicing the bank’s loans until the disagreement is settled. Which of the following best describes what the dispute resolution provision of the agreement should have contained?

options.A: Express choice-of-law and jurisdictional terms, so that any disagreement is adjudicated under the laws of a single, specific jurisdiction.
options.B: Suspension of all services until the dispute is resolved, so that neither party is prejudiced by continuing to perform during the disagreement.
options.C: Referral of every disagreement to litigation in the institution’s home courts, so that each dispute ends with an enforceable judgment.
options.D: A process to expedite problem resolution that also addresses the continuation of the arrangement between the parties during the dispute resolution period.

solution:
CCO facing a billing dispute in which the domestic subservicer threatens to stop servicing.

**Concept and theory**

In an outsourcing relationship a disagreement can do more damage than the amount in dispute, because the provider controls a service the institution depends on. The **dispute resolution** provision addresses both the disagreement and the service. GARP: agreements should include a dispute resolution process in order to (1) expedite problem resolution and (2) address the continuation of the arrangement between the parties during the dispute resolution period. The second purpose is the distinctive one: the clause is designed so that a billing or performance dispute does not interrupt the outsourced activity.

It is distinct from the foreign-based service provider provision, which concerns which law and jurisdiction govern disputes with a provider located abroad.

**Applying it to this question**

The subservicer is domestic, so choice of law across borders is not the issue. The threat to stop servicing is exactly the risk the second limb of the provision addresses. The right description must combine speed of resolution with continuation of the arrangement.

**Fragile fact.** Dispute resolution has two jobs: expedite resolution and keep the arrangement running during the dispute; choice of law is a different provision.

question:
The chief risk officer of the U.S. operations of an Australian banking group, which reports to its parent in AUD, is reviewing a fund administration provider’s proposal to cap its contractual liability. The figures below have been converted into AUD.

| Item | AUD million |
|---|---|
| Annual fees payable to the provider | 0.9 |
| Proposed liability cap (12 months of fees) | 0.9 |
| Estimated loss to the institution if the provider fails to perform | 45.0 |

The provider employs about 1,200 staff across three countries. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: The provider’s board should judge whether the cap is reasonable relative to the fees the provider earns, since the cap limits the provider’s own exposure.
options.B: The institution’s legal counsel alone should approve the cap, since a limitation on liability is a legal drafting matter rather than a risk decision.
options.C: The institution’s board of directors and senior management should determine whether the cap is reasonable when compared to the risks to the institution if the provider fails to perform.
options.D: The institution should reject the cap outright, since the guidance does not permit service providers to limit their liability contractually.

CRO of an Australian group’s U.S. operations evaluating a provider’s proposed liability cap.

Providers commonly seek to cap their exposure, typically at a multiple of fees. A low cap shifts the residual loss from a provider failure back onto the institution. The **limits on liability** provision does not forbid caps; it assigns the decision and sets the test. GARP: service providers may want to contractually limit their liability. The board of directors and senior management of the financial institution should determine whether the proposed limitations are reasonable when compared to the risks to the institution if a service provider fails to perform.

This fits the wider principle in Section 12.3: using service providers does not relieve the board and senior management of responsibility for outsourced activities, so a decision that leaves residual risk with the institution belongs at that level.

question: A junior risk analyst at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing an agreement under which a provider runs the call centre that receives and resolves complaints from the bank’s credit card customers. Which of the following draft clauses is most consistent with the guidance?

options.A: The agreement specifies each party’s responsibilities for responding to complaints and, as the provider resolves them, requires it to give the bank summary reports tracking their status and resolution.
options.B: The agreement assigns all complaint handling to the bank, since the guidance does not allow a service provider to take responsibility for resolving customer complaints.
options.C: The agreement requires the provider, which resolves the complaints, to report to the bank only those complaints that have escalated into litigation or regulatory action.
options.D: The agreement requires the bank to send the provider summary reports tracking the status and resolution of complaints, since the provider is the party resolving them.

solution:
Junior risk analyst reviewing complaint-handling terms for an outsourced call centre.

**Concept and theory**

Customers experience the institution through whoever answers the phone. When a provider deals with customers, the institution still bears the reputational and regulatory consequences of how complaints are handled, so it needs both clarity of roles and visibility. The **customer** **complaints** provision supplies both. GARP: agreements should specify the responsibilities of financial institutions and service providers related to responding to customer complaints. If service providers are responsible for customer complaint resolution, agreements should provide for summary reports to the financial institutions that track the status and resolution of complaints.

**Applying it to this question**

The provider resolves complaints, so the conditional limb applies. The correct clause must (1) allocate responsibilities between both parties, (2) have reports flow from provider to bank, and (3) cover status and resolution of complaints in general, not a subset.

**Fragile fact.** If the provider resolves complaints, it reports to the institution, and the reports track both status and resolution.

options.B: The agreement should provide for disputes to be adjudicated under the laws of both countries at once, so that each party is protected in its home courts.

Contracts are only as good as their enforceability. With a provider abroad, two legal systems may claim jurisdiction, and foreign law may treat contract enforcement differently from U.S. law. The **foreign-based service providers** provision addresses this. GARP:

- institutions should consider including express choice of law and jurisdictional provisions that would provide for the adjudication of all disputes between the two parties under the laws of a single, specific jurisdiction;

question: An internal auditor at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing an incident at its document imaging provider. With the bank’s consent, the provider subcontracted the indexing of scanned files to a firm in another country, and that firm mishandled customer data. The provider argues that the subcontractor alone is responsible. Which of the following statements is most accurate?

options.A: The primary provider has overall accountability for all services provided by it and its subcontractors, and the same contractual provisions should apply to the subcontractor.
options.B: Accountability for the subcontracted indexing passes to the subcontractor, since it performed the work and the institution consented to the subcontracting arrangement.
options.C: The subcontractor is bound only by those provisions that the primary provider chooses to pass on, provided the primary provider remains accountable to the institution.
options.D: The primary provider’s accountability extends only to domestic subcontractors, since a foreign subcontractor’s work is governed by its home jurisdiction’s standards.

Internal auditor reviewing a data incident at a foreign subcontractor of the document imaging provider.

Subcontracting creates a chain: institution, primary provider, subcontractor. The institution has a contract only with the primary provider, so without explicit terms the controls it negotiated could disappear one link down the chain. The **subcontracting** provision closes that gap with two core rules. GARP: if agreements allow for subcontracting, the same contractual provisions should apply to the subcontractor; and contract provisions should clearly state that the primary service provider has overall accountability for all services that the service provider and its subcontractors provide. GARP adds that institutions should pay special attention to foreign subcontractors, as information security and data privacy standards may differ in other jurisdictions.

The result is that the institution can always look to one accountable counterparty, and that the subcontractor is held to the institution’s standards.

The provider’s argument (“the subcontractor alone is responsible”) is exactly what the accountability rule prevents. The fact that the institution consented and that the subcontractor is foreign changes nothing about accountability; the foreign location is a reason for extra attention, not an exemption.

I. The services that may be subcontracted.

II. The provider’s due diligence process for engaging and monitoring subcontractors.

III. A standing consent allowing the provider to change its subcontractors without notifying the institution, provided the services remain within the agreed scope.

IV. The provider’s process for assessing a subcontractor’s financial condition to fulfil the contractual obligations.

Which of the items should the agreement include?

options.A: I and II only
options.B: II and III only
options.C: I, II and IV only
options.D: I, II, III and IV

solution:
Risk committee member checking four items in a subcontracting provision.

**Concept and theory**

Beyond the accountability and flow-down rules (Q18), the **subcontracting** provision specifies what the agreement should define. GARP: agreements should define (1) the services that may be subcontracted;

(2) the service provider’s due diligence process for engaging and monitoring subcontractors;

(3) the notification and approval requirements regarding changes to the service provider’s subcontractors;

and agreements should include (4) the service provider’s process for assessing the subcontractor’s financial condition to fulfil contractual obligations. Each item keeps the institution informed and in control of who actually performs its work. The notification and approval requirement matters most in practice: without it, the institution’s due diligence on the original subcontractor could become obsolete overnight.

**Applying it to this question**

Items I, II and IV are GARP’s items (1), (2) and (4). Item III, a standing consent to change subcontractors without notice, removes item (3), the notification and approval requirement. The answer is I, II and IV.

**Fragile fact.** Changes to subcontractors require notification and approval; the provider’s own process for assessing subcontractors’ financial condition goes into the agreement.

| Product sold by the agency | Commission (% of balance) |
|---|---|
| Standard savings account | 0.25 |
| Structured deposit (higher margin to the bank) | 1.50 |

In addition, the agency receives a fixed monthly retainer of USD 20,000. Which of the following responses is most appropriate?

GARP’s example of an inappropriate incentive is one where variable fees or commissions encourage the provider to direct customers to products with higher profit margins without due consideration of whether they are suitable. question: A senior risk analyst at a U.S. bank holding company is reviewing the draft agreement with a provider that internal assessments rate as higher risk following recent control weaknesses. Which of the following draft clauses best supports the bank’s ongoing oversight of this provider?

options.A: The provider must deliver its annual financial statements, give additional reporting in view of its higher risk, and accept increased monitoring if performance, control or viability concerns arise.
options.B: The frequency of the bank’s monitoring is fixed at signing and cannot be increased during the term, so as to give the provider certainty over its compliance costs.
options.C: The bank must deliver its own annual financial statements to the provider, so that the provider can monitor the bank’s ability to continue paying for the service.
options.D: The provider receives the same level of monitoring as the bank’s lower-risk providers, since its suitability was already established through due diligence before signing.

solution:
Senior risk analyst choosing an oversight clause for a higher-risk provider.

**Concept and theory**

Schweser lists **oversight and monitoring** as a contract provision: the contract should require the provider to deliver annual financial statements (and annual report, if applicable) so that the institution can monitor its ability to continue as a going concern; it should allow the institution to increase monitoring and oversight when performance deficiencies, control weaknesses or viability concerns are noted; and for higher-risk providers it could stipulate extra reporting by the provider or additional monitoring by the institution. GARP covers the same content as a programme element (part E): the oversight process should be risk-focused; higher-risk providers may require more frequent assessment and monitoring and tailored risk mitigation plans, which may include additional reporting by the provider or heightened monitoring by the institution; more frequent and stringent monitoring is needed for providers with performance, financial, compliance or control concerns; institutions should monitor the financial condition of providers by reviewing their most recent financial statements and annual report; and risk management processes should include triggers to escalate oversight. Lower-risk providers can be monitored less.

|---|---|---|
| 1 | Proof of insurance; notify material change in coverage | Insurance |
| 2 | Express choice of law and jurisdiction; a single, specific jurisdiction for a provider abroad | Foreign-based service providers |

| 4 | Opportunities for curing default; termination rights | Default and termination |

loText: Explain how risks related to the use of third parties can arise and describe characteristics of an effective third-party risk management framework.
question: A junior risk analyst at a Singapore private bank is drafting a glossary for the operational risk committee. The committee has asked for an entry that defines third-party risk management (TPRM) and explains how the term “third-party risk” relates to “outsourcing risk”. Which of the following entries is most accurate?

options.A: Third-party risk is the narrower term, covering only activities formally outsourced by the bank, while outsourcing risk covers all risks arising from external providers.
options.B: Outsourcing risk relates to activities outsourced to third parties, while third-party risk is the more general term covering all risks from third parties that can affect the bank.
options.C: Third parties are limited to providers of outsourced services under a formal contract, so suppliers of goods and business partners fall outside the scope of TPRM.
options.D: TPRM covers the identification, assessment and monitoring of third-party risks, while the mitigation of those risks passes to the provider under the contract.

solution:
Junior analyst at a Singapore private bank defining TPRM and relating “third-party risk” to “outsourcing risk”.

**Concept and theory**

Third-party risk management (TPRM) is the identification, assessment, mitigation and monitoring, by an organisation, of the risks that arise from its use of third parties. A third party is any provider of goods or services that is not internal to the firm: vendors, suppliers, partners, contractors and service providers. The definition is deliberately wide. It is not limited to formal outsourcing of a business process; a supplier of goods or a business partner can expose the firm to loss just as an outsourced back office can.

Two labels are used for the same family of risks:

| Term | Scope |
|---|---|
| Outsourcing risk | Risks of activities that the firm has outsourced to third parties (the narrower term) |
| Third-party risk | All risks arising from third parties that can affect the client institution (the more general term) |

In practice the two are used quite interchangeably, but strictly third-party risk is the broader concept, because a firm can be exposed to a third party (a supplier, a partner) without having outsourced an activity to it. The “M” in TPRM matters: the framework is not only about spotting and watching risk, it includes mitigating it, and that duty stays with the client firm.

question: A treasury analyst at a Canadian credit union is preparing a business case for moving back-office reconciliations and cloud-based data management to a specialist provider. The projected saving is CAD 1.8 million a year. A board member asks how the move will affect the credit union’s operational risk. Which of the following responses is most accurate?

options.A: The move transfers the operational risk of these activities to the provider, so the credit union’s operational risk exposure from them falls to zero.
options.B: The move may reduce costs, but because the work leaves the credit union it cannot reduce its process errors or its cybersecurity risk.
options.C: The move may reduce process errors, and the third-party risk it creates can be managed with the controls already used for the work in-house.
options.D: The move may reduce process errors or cybersecurity risk, but it does not fully mitigate operational risk and adds third-party risk with its own challenges.

solution:
Treasury analyst at a Canadian credit union asked how outsourcing back-office and cloud data work affects operational risk.

**Concept and theory**

Firms contract with third parties for two broad reasons. The first is cost: activities are outsourced to specialised firms that have a competitive advantage in particular systems, processes and knowledge. The second is risk: engaging a specialist can be an operational risk mitigation strategy, because back-office or cloud-based data management by an expert may reduce process errors or cybersecurity risk.

The catch is what outsourcing does to the risk profile overall. It does not fully mitigate operational risk. It also creates a new exposure, third-party risk, which has its own management challenges: the firm must now select, contract with, monitor and, if needed, exit the provider, and it depends on controls it does not run itself. So the net effect is a change in the shape of operational risk, not its removal.

| Effect | What outsourcing does |
|---|---|
| Cost | Can save costs through specialisation |
| Process and cyber risk | May be reduced by a specialist provider |
| Operational risk overall | Not fully mitigated |
| Third-party risk | Increased, with its own management challenges |
